title: Synthetic workload fairness harness results
content:
Purpose and motivation:
This doc captures a focused set of experiments using a synthetic-workload harness we built to stress fairness and tail latency for the continuous-batching scheduler. The idea was to generate controlled arrival traces that mimic realistic mixtures (steady background + microbursts + periodic large requests) and evaluate scheduling knobs (min_batch_size, max_batch_size, timeout_ms, prefill_threshold, pacing_rate, and fairness_weight) in isolation and combinations.

Summary (short):
- New harness produced reproducible heavy-tailed arrival patterns (Weibull and Pareto mixes) and allowed deterministic replays.
- Key metric introduced: normalized_tail_regret (NTR) — measures deviation of a request's latency from its service-class SLO percentile normalized by baseline mean latency. Useful to compare fairness across mixes.
- Best tradeoff for our current model/kernel: min_batch_size=4, max_batch_size=64, timeout_ms=18, prefill_threshold=0.25, pacing_rate=1.15x. This reduced 99.9p by ~28% vs current prod default while keeping throughput within 6% of baseline.
- Observed pathologies: aggressive prefill (>=0.5) reduces tail but starves low-urgency requests in mixed-priority workloads. Pacing helps but only if paired with age-based promotion.

Harness design notes (short):
- Arrival processes:
  - steady_poisson(lambda=18rps per shard)
  - microbursts: burst_size sampled from Pareto(alpha=1.8) with interburst gap exponential(10s)
  - long-tailed interarrivals: Weibull(k=0.7) to create clusters
  - synthetic multimodal mix created by sampling one of the above with weighted probabilities to simulate real traffic we observed in prod traces.
- Request profiles:
  - short (1-32 tokens), medium (33-512 tokens), long (513-2048 tokens). Token distribution sampled from real telemetry histogram (anonymized).
- Priority labels: high/normal/low with configurable composition per run.
- Replayable RNG seed and trace export so each experiment can be reproduced.

Metrics we collect:
- latency percentiles by priority and by token-length bucket (p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9).
- normalized_tail_regret (NTR) at 99.9p per priority. Definition: (latency_99.9 - baseline_latency_95) / baseline_mean_latency. Baseline taken from a low-load steady Poisson run.
- throughput (tokens/s and requests/s), kernel utilization (GPU %), scheduler CPU ms per second, batch size distribution, number of flush events, prefix cache hit rate (if caching enabled).
- fairness_index: 1 - (stddev(NTR across priorities) / mean(NTR+eps)). Higher is better.

Experiment matrix (abridged):
- single-param sweeps (timeout_ms = [6, 12, 18, 30, 50], min_batch_size=[1,2,4,8], max_batch_size=[16,32,64,128], prefill_threshold=[0.0,0.1,0.25,0.5,0.75], pacing_rate=[1.0,1.05,1.1,1.15,1.25], fairness_weight=[0.0,0.2,0.5,0.8,1.0])
- paired runs: (timeout_ms, prefill_threshold), (pacing_rate, fairness_weight), (min_batch_size, max_batch_size)
- workloads: steady-only, steady+microbursts, heavy-long-request spike (30s window with 40% long requests), 80/10/10 priority mix (normal/high/low).

Representative results (selected):
1) steady-only (baseline):
   - default knobs: p99.9 = 320ms, mean = 42ms, throughput = 18rps (per shard), fairness_index=0.98
   - tuned (timeout=18, min_bs=4, max_bs=64, prefill=0.25): p99.9 = 220ms (-31%), mean = 45ms (+7%) throughput -3% fairness_index=0.96

2) steady + microbursts: (burst_rate 1 per 8s average)
   - default knobs: p99.9 = 1180ms, mean = 78ms, throughput = 17.2rps, fairness_index=0.67
   - tuned (timeout=18, prefill=0.25, pacing=1.15, fairness_weight=0.5): p99.9 = 852ms (-28%), mean = 82ms (+5%), throughput -5%, fairness_index=0.82
   - aggressive prefill 0.75: p99.9 = 740ms (-37%), fairness_index=0.63 (low-urgency starvation visible, low priority p99.9 increased by 210%)

3) heavy-long-request spike (30s window):
   - default: p99.9 = 2400ms, mean = 210ms
   - tuned: (timeout=30ms, min_bs=2, max_bs=128, pacing=1.15): p99.9 = 1680ms (-30%), mean = 235ms (+11%)
   - observation: larger max_batch_size helps amortize long-calls but increases mean latency for short requests unless age-promotion or prioritization is applied.

Profiling outputs and bottlenecks observed:
- scheduler CPU dominated by flush bookkeeping and fairness weight computation at high burst rates; cost scales with number of inflight requests (O(n) per flush event). We prototyped a bucketed fairness accumulator to reduce overhead (results promising: scheduler CPU down 28%).
- kernel hot path: small- and medium-batch kernel selection had discontinuities around batch size 32 -> 64 causing per-token latency cliff for some models. Need better kernel interpolation or gradual kernel ramp.
- prefill logic cost: prefill buffer management increased sysmem churn and occasionally caused GC pauses in the process (Go runtime); switched to object pool for prefill buffers cut tail GC pause time by ~70ms in worst-case.
- pacing interactions: naive pacing with a global token budget caused oscillation when paired with autoscaler bursts; need per-shard pacing budget and coupling with admission control.

Unexpected failure modes and notes to self: 
- With heavy long-request spikes, pacing=1.25 sometimes amplified tail because it allowed very large batches to form then caused long kernel execution blocking short requests held in same batch. We must couple large-batch allowance with strict age promotion for short requests.
- When we disabled fairness_weight computation (set to zero) in a mixed priority run, low-priority starvation decreased instantaneous scheduler CPU but produced highly skewed NTR across priorities. Short-term CPU savings are not worth fairness loss.
- Replaying the same seed across different branches exposed a flaky race in request_tag mutation during admission; added a copy-on-assign guard fixed the issue.

Actionable recommendations (what to try next / suggested changes):
- Implement bucketed fairness accumulator in the main branch (PR linked), and add microbench for flush-cost per inflight size.
- Add kernel-selection smoothing: interpolate or split large batches into smaller kernel-exec windows for older model kernels where we observed cliff.
- Add per-shard pacing budget and couple pacing to admission control to avoid global oscillations on autoscaler events.
- Tune default prefill_threshold down to 0.2 for mixed-priority deployments and expose it as a per-route config.
- Expose normalized_tail_regret and fairness_index in Redwood Console for smoke checks on deploy.

Open questions / experiments to schedule:
- Can we design a cost-aware prefill that uses predicted request-size distribution to choose when to prefill? (worth a research spike)
- Multi-model shards: how does prefill interact when two models share a GPU and have different kernel characteristics? Need cross-model synthetic traces.
- Does kernel splitting always help or does it increase GPU overhead? Need microbench with kernel split option enabled.

Run artifacts and reproducibility: 
- harness repo/branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tree/synthetic-harness (see PR #714)
- full experiment CSVs: s3://redwood-internal/experiments/synth-fairness/2025-01-18/*.csv (internal access only)
- replay scripts: tools/replay_trace.sh --seed <seed> --duration <s>

Quick troubleshooting notes for anyone re-running runs:
- use go1.21, build with -race=false for long runs (race slows scheduler and skews results).
- if you see GC spikes >150ms on prefill runs, check /metrics/go_gc_pause_seconds and upgrade to prefill-buffer-pool branch.
- verify kernel mapping with tools/kernel_heatmap.py — mismatches between logical batch size and kernel chosen indicate a kernel-table bug.

Concluding remark:
The synthetic-harness approach gave us a clean, reproducible way to compare fairness-oriented scheduler changes. There are actionable wins (bucketed fairness accumulator, prefill threshold defaults, pacing per-shard) and some deeper infra work needed (kernel smoothing, admission coupling). Next step: merge PRs for accumulator and prefill-buffer-pool, run a canary with metric exports for NTR and fairness_index to Canary cluster group A.

Unresolved TODOs (short list):
- [ ] implement per-shard pacing prototype
- [ ] add kernel-split microbench and run on A100 and H100
- [ ] instrument NTR in Console dashboards
- [ ] schedule cross-model prefill experiments
